deep.reconstruction:
Setting. This is Casus II of Euler's friction theory. Water flows steadily from a very large reservoir (cross-section ff, height a, kept full) through a narrow vertical cylinder BC (section gg, length b). It then passes into a second vertical cylinder CD (section hh, length c) and leaves through an orifice DD = kk into air. l is the atmospheric pressure expressed as a water-column height, and v is the velocity head (height due to the efflux velocity) at the orifice. By continuity, the velocity head in a pipe of section gg is (k^4/g^4)v, written 𝔤v; in pipe hh it is 𝔥v; in the reservoir it is k^4/f^4 times v, which is neglected.

Friction law. Euler's hypothesis is that wall friction is proportional to the local pressure p (in head units) times perimeter over area, i.e. proportional to p/f, p/g, p/h. Within each cylinder the velocity is constant, so the pressure obeys dp/dx = 1 − αp/(width). Integrating gives p_end = p_start·e^{−αL/w} + w(1 − e^{−αL/w})/α. This is the origin of the abbreviations 𝔄 = e^{−αa/f}, A = (1−𝔄)/α, and the analogous 𝔅, B, ℭ, C.

Derivation (my reconstruction, which reproduces the printed formula).
- Reservoir: p_B = l𝔄 + Af.
- Entering BC, the pressure drops by the velocity head 𝔤v.
- At C: p_C = (l𝔄 + Af − 𝔤v)𝔅 + Bg.
- Entering CD, there is a lossless Bernoulli change: −(𝔥 − 𝔤)v.
- At D: p_D = [p_C − (𝔥 − 𝔤)v]ℭ + Ch.
- At the orifice: p_D + 𝔥v = l + v.

Solving for v gives
v = [A𝔅ℭf + Bℭg + Ch − (1 − 𝔄𝔅ℭ)l] / [1 − (1−𝔅)ℭ𝔤 − (1−ℭ)𝔥],
exactly as printed. As α → 0, A → a, B → b, C → c and all exponential factors → 1, so v → a + b + c: the Torricelli head equals the total height AD.

§69 starts the discussion of when this case is genuinely new. If gg = hh the problem reduces to Case I. Otherwise BC must be much narrower than both neighbours, and then (on the next page) vena-contracta effects are absorbed by lengthening b and shortening a and c.
errors: Physically, the hypothesis that friction is proportional to absolute pressure is incorrect for fluids. It makes atmospheric pressure l enter v through the term −(1−𝔄𝔅ℭ)l, predicting that efflux decreases as ambient pressure rises. This is contrary to experience; the algebra itself is consistent.

The transition from the narrow pipe BC to the wide pipe CD is treated as lossless Bernoulli pressure recovery (the term −(𝔥−𝔤)v). The sudden-expansion (Borda–Carnot) loss is ignored, and Euler instead blames all the observed slowing on friction (§69).
No algebraic error found: the formula and the α→0 limit check out.

ideas.what: Steady one-dimensional pipe flow with wall friction proportional to local pressure, integrated piecewise with exponential transfer factors across cylinders in series.
ideas.modern_name: Pressure-dependent (Coulomb-type) wall friction in a hydraulic network; transfer-matrix style composition of pipe segments
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler's own (abandoned) hypothesis; modern pipe friction stems from Chézy (1770s), Darcy–Weisbach (19th c.)
ideas.where_published: E260 itself (Novi Comment. Acad. Sci. Petrop. 6, 1761); discussed in the Opera omnia II.13 editorial introduction (Truesdell) — details unsure

ideas.what: Torricelli limit v = a+b+c when friction vanishes, independent of pipe sections.
ideas.modern_name: Bernoulli/Torricelli efflux for a compound pipe
ideas.where_published: E260; Euler's hydraulic memoirs of the 1750s

ideas.what: Accounting for vena contracta at contractions/expansions by an effective change of segment lengths (begun at the end of §69, carried out §70–71).

deep.surprise_reason: This is a correct, routine application of Euler's (physically mistaken) pressure-proportional friction law to two pipes in series. The model and its fate are known from Euler-scholarship accounts of E260, and nothing here seems to be absent from the literature.
transcription_corrections: 'quae fit valde magna' should read 'quae sit valde magna'.
The exponents are printed as e^{-αa/f}, e^{-αb/g}, e^{-αc/h}; the transcription is correct.
The page footer 'sin' is the catchword for 'ſin autem' beginning the next page.
